auth.title: Authorization — Ramp API docs
highlights:
Authorization

Ramp uses OAuth 2.0. Your app gets an access token from `/developer/v1/token`, authenticating with its client ID and secret (typically HTTP Basic Auth), and scopes control what the token can access.

For a quick start, see the Setup Guide. For Ramp's own MCP server and CLI, see Ramp MCP and Ramp CLI.

## Supported grant types

| Grant Type | Use Case | User Interaction |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Client Credentials | Internal integrations, server-to-server | None required |
| Authorization Code | Third-party apps, public integrations | Authorized user consent required |
| Refresh Token | Renew access after an Authorization Code grant | None after the initial authorization |

## Permission model and scopes

Scopes follow the pattern `resource:permission`, where the permission is usually `read` or `write`, such as `transactions:read`. A few use other permissions, such as `cards:read_vault`. OpenID Connect scopes, such as `openid` and `offline_access`, don't follow the pattern.

Request only the scopes your app needs. Each endpoint's API reference lists its required scopes. The table below lists common scopes and isn't exhaustive.

| Scope | Resource | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `accounting:read` | Accounting data | Access accounting sync status and metadata |

...

`cards:read_vault` is available only to approved integrators; see Virtual Cards. Scopes marked partners only appear in the partner Developer Console, not in a business's own Developer API settings. Some endpoints also require a Ramp plan feature and return `403` without it, even with the right scope.

...

## Token management

- Format: Access tokens are bearer tokens prefixed with `ramp_business_tok_`, `ramp_user_tok_`, `ramp_business_jwt_`, or `ramp_user_jwt_`.
- Lifetime: Client Credentials access tokens last 10 days (864,000 seconds). Authorization Code and Refresh Token access tokens default to 1 hour (3,600 seconds), and some apps have a different configured lifetime. Use `expires_in` from the token response.
- Scopes: A token can't be used beyond its granted scopes. To change scopes, get a new token. Ramp MCP and Ramp CLI tokens are limited by the user's role and access level instead.
- Environment: Tokens work only in the environment that issued them. Sandbox and production need separate apps.

Treat tokens as credentials

Never log tokens or include them in error messages, store them encrypted, and send them only over HTTPS.

## Authorization flows

### Client credentials flow

Use this flow for server-to-server integrations with your own Ramp business. Send `client_id:client_secret`, base64-encoded, in an `Authorization: Basic ...` header. Some apps are configured to send `client_id` and `client_secret` in the form body instead.

Pass the scopes you need as a space-separated `scope` field. If you omit `scope`, the token has no scopes. The token has business-wide access limited by those scopes, and there's no end user. Actions that need a user are attributed to the app's creator by default.

Client Credentials doesn't return a refresh token. Request a new access token when the current one expires. Keep the client secret on your servers, never in client-side code.

### Authorization code flow

Permanent link: Authorization code flow

Use this flow when other Ramp businesses or users grant your app access, such as apps listed on ramp.com/integrations.

#### Step 1: Redirect the user to Ramp

Send the user to Ramp's authorization URL with these parameters:

- `response_type` Required — Must be `code`.
- `scope` Required — Space-separated list of scopes, such as `transactions:read business:read`.
- `client_id` Required — Your app's client ID from the Ramp Developer Console↗.
- `redirect_uri` Required — Must exactly match a redirect URI configured for your app, including the path. Use `https://`, or `http://` only for `localhost` or `127.0.0.1`.
- `state` Required — A random value your app verifies on return, to protect against CSRF. Required for apps created after June 15, 2023, and recommended for all apps.

https://app.ramp.com/v1/authorize?response_type=code&client_id=YOUR_CLIENT_ID&redirect_uri=https://yourapp.com/callback&scope=transactions:read business:read&state=random_csrf_token

Use the builder below to generate a correctly encoded URL. It uses `https://demo.ramp.com/v1/authorize` for sandbox and `https://app.ramp.com/v1/authorize` for production. No client secret is needed.

Build your authorization URL

Use the client ID and registered callback URI from this environment.

Your app's client ID, not its client secret.

Must exactly match a redirect URI registered for your app. Paste the URI without URL-encoding it first.

Enter space-separated scopes enabled for your app and available to the business you are authorizing.

Use a cryptographically random value for each authorization attempt. Store it in your app and verify it on the callback.

`Your authorization URL will appear here once all required fields are valid.`

#### Step 2: The user approves access

Permanent link: Step 2: The user approves access

The user signs in to Ramp and approves your app's requested access.

Who can approve

For apps that access the whole business, an Admin or Business Owner must approve. Other users see "An admin must connect this app." For apps that act as an individual user, an admin must first enable the app for the organization in Manage Access.

Ramp then redirects to your `redirect_uri` with a `code` and the original `state`. If the user denies access, the redirect includes `error=access_denied` instead.

https://yourapp.com/callback?code=AUTH_CODE_HERE&state=random_csrf_token

#### Step 3: Exchange the `code` for an access token

Permanent link: Step 3: Exchange the `code` for an access token

Codes expire after 5 minutes.

Exchange code for access token

Shell

Copy

curl --request POST '{environment-url}/developer/v1/token' \

 --header "Authorization: Basic $(echo -n "$CLIENT_ID:$CLIENT_SECRET" | base64)" \

 --header "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" \

 --data-urlencode "grant_type=authorization_code" \

 --data-urlencode "code=AUTH_CODE_HERE" \

 --data-urlencode "redirect_uri=https://yourapp.com/callback"

#### Step 4: Refresh the access token

Permanent link: Step 4: Refresh the access token

To get refresh tokens, enable the Refresh Token grant type for your app. Then exchange the refresh token for a new access token:

curl --request POST '{environment-url}/developer/v1/token' \

 --header "Authorization: Basic $(echo -n "$CLIENT_ID:$CLIENT_SECRET" | base64)" \

 --header 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' \

 --data-urlencode 'grant_type=refresh_token' \

 --data-urlencode 'refresh_token=REFRESH_TOKEN_HERE'

The response has a new access token but no new refresh token. Keep using the original refresh token until it expires or is revoked, then restart the Authorization Code flow. `refresh_token_expires_in` is returned with the original refresh token only if your app has a configured refresh-token lifetime; refreshing doesn't extend it.

### Revoke an access or refresh token

Send the token to `POST /developer/v1/token/revoke`, with the same Basic Auth credentials you use to create tokens. A successful request returns HTTP `200`.

curl --request POST 'https://api.ramp.com/developer/v1/token/revoke' \

 --header "Authorization: Basic $(echo -n "$CLIENT_ID:$CLIENT_SECRET" | base64)" \

 --header 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' \

 --data-urlencode "token=$RAMP_API_TOKEN"

## Error handling

### Token request errors

Failed requests to `/developer/v1/token` return HTTP `400` with error code `DEVELOPER_7012` and one of these messages:

| Message | What to check |
| --- | --- |
| Client authentication failed. | Client ID and secret, and the environment |
| The provided authorization grant or refresh token is invalid. | The code expired, was already used, or the `redirect_uri` doesn't match; or the refresh token expired or was revoked |
| The requested scope is invalid, unknown, malformed, or exceeds the scope granted by the resource owner. | Request only scopes configured for your app |
| The authenticated client is not authorized to use this authorization grant type. | Enable the grant type in your app settings |

If the client credentials are missing or malformed, the request returns HTTP `401`.

### API errors

- 401 Unauthorized: The token is missing, expired, or invalid.
- 403 Forbidden: The token lacks a required scope. For Ramp MCP and Ramp CLI, the user's role doesn't allow the action, or the connection is read-only and the request makes a change (`DEVELOPER_7100`). Some role errors from these tools return `400` with the message `You do not have the required permissions to use this tool`.
- 429 Too Many Requests: See Rate Limiting.

auth.title: Quickstart — Ramp API docs
highlights:
This guide assumes you are a Ramp customer with admin access to your dashboard. Need a test environment for development? Request sandbox access.

## 1. Create your app and get credentials

Permanent link: 1. Create your app and get credentials

First, you'll need to create a developer app to get your API credentials.

1. In your Ramp account, go to Company → Developer (you'll need admin access).
2. Click Create New App.
3. Name your app (e.g., "API Quickstart") and accept the Terms.
4. Under Grant types, click Add new grant type → select Client Credentials.
5. Under Scopes, click Configure allowed scopes and select `transactions:read`.
6. Copy your Client ID and Client Secret. Store them securely – you'll need them in the next step.

For more details on authorization, see the Authorization Guide.

Your browser does not support the video tag.

## 2. Get an access token

With your credentials, request an access token. Ramp authenticates this `/developer/v1/token` request with HTTP Basic Auth: base64-encode `client_id:client_secret` and send it in the `Authorization` header. The token authenticates your API requests.

Replace `{environment-url}` with:

- `https://demo-api.ramp.com` for Sandbox
- `https://api.ramp.com` for Production

API URLs are different from the Ramp app URLs

The API base URL is not the same as the URL for the Ramp customer app. Make sure you're pointing your API calls at the API host, not the frontend host.

| Environment | API base URL | Ramp app URL |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Production | `https://api.ramp.com` | `https://app.ramp.com` |
| Sandbox (demo) | `https://demo-api.ramp.com` | `https://demo.ramp.com` |

Copy

curl -X POST '{environment-url}/developer/v1/token' \

 -H "Authorization: Basic $(echo -n "$CLIENT_ID:$CLIENT_SECRET" | base64)" \

 -H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" \

 -d "grant_type=client_credentials" \

 -d "scope=transactions:read"

Response:

 " access_token": "ramp_business_tok_abc123...",

 " token_type": "Bearer",

 " expires_in": 864000,

 " scope": "transactions:read"

Store the `access_token` securely – you'll use it to make API calls. Run the token request in your backend or local development environment; do not expose the client secret in browser code. Use `expires_in` to determine how long the token is valid, in seconds. Client Credentials access tokens expire after 10 days. Client Credentials grants do not return a refresh token; request a new access token when the current token expires.

The `scope` parameter is required for this example. If you omit it from a Client Credentials request, Ramp issues a token with no scopes, which cannot call the Transactions endpoint.

## 3. Make your first API call

With your access token, you can now call the Ramp API. Let's retrieve your transactions using the GET /transactions endpoint.

Add the header `Authorization: Bearer <YOUR_TOKEN_HERE>` and make a GET request to `{environment-url}/developer/v1/transactions`.

Get transactions

curl -X GET '{environment-url}/developer/v1/transactions' \

 -H "Authorization: Bearer $ACCESS_TOKEN"

auth.title: Ramp API docs
highlights:
Authorization

Before using the API, you'll need to set up authorization. To quickly get started, refer to our Setup Guide.

## Create a token

Expects two headers:

- Authorization header formed from base-64 encoded client credentials as `Authorization: Basic <base64-encoded client_id:client_secret>`
- `Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded`

Required content body depends on authorization type method, as defined by `grant_type`.

- Authorization Code Grant (`grant_type=authorization_code`): `grant_type`, `code`, and `redirect_uri` are required. Request must happen after requested scopes have been approved and exchanged for authorization code.
- Refresh Token Grant (`grant_type=refresh_token`): `grant_type` and `refresh_token` are required. User must have previously obtained refresh token in authorization code flow.
- Client Credentials Grant (`grant_type=client_credentials`): `grant_type` is required. If `scope` is omitted, the access token has no scopes.
- JWT Bearer Grant (`grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer`): `grant_type` and an ID-JAG `assertion` are required. Issues a user-level access token without a refresh token.

## Request body

`grant_type`  string

Grant type, must be one of: ['authorization_code', 'client_credentials', 'refresh_token', 'urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer']. Refresh token and client credentials grants must be added to app's permitted Grant Types.

 Allowed values 

`assertion`  string

optional

ID-JAG JWT assertion for the JWT bearer grant.

`code`  string

optional

Authorization code obtained from request to https://app.ramp.com/v1/authorize, to be exchanged for access token. Field is required if grant_type=authorization_code.

`redirect_uri`  string

optional

The redirect URI previously used in the authorization request, used to verify app. Field is required if grant_type=authorization_code.

`refresh_token`  string

optional

The refresh token issued to you to get a new access token.

`scope`  string

Space-separated list of scopes to be granted to the returned token. These must be a subset (including full set) of the app's allowed scopes. If omitted for grant_type=client_credentials, the returned token has no scopes.

## Response HTTP 200

`access_token`  string

optional

The access token string. Prefixed with ramp_business_tok_, ramp_user_tok_, ramp_business_jwt_, or ramp_user_jwt_.

`expires_in`  integer

optional

The duration of which the token is valid, measured in seconds.

`id_token`  string

optional

An OpenID Connect ID token.

`refresh_token`  string

Refresh token can be used to get a new access token. Note that refresh token won't appear in the response for client_credentials grant type. Prefixed with ramp_business_tok_ or ramp_user_tok_.

`refresh_token_expires_in`  integer or null

optional

The duration of which the refresh token is valid, measured in seconds. This field only appears for clients configured with a refresh token TTL and only when a refresh token is returned.

`resource`  string or null

optional

Protected resource the access token is bound to.

`scope`  string

Space-separated list of scopes of the access token.

The type of the token. This should always be 'Bearer'.

Copy

curl --request POST

gate.title: Partner Integrations — Ramp API docs
highlights:
Partner Integrations

Ramp enables technology partners to build integrations that reach 50,000+ businesses. This guide walks you through building, testing, and publicly listing on the Ramp Integrations page↗.

## Why build on Ramp?

Permanent link: Why build on Ramp?

- Monetize your integration — You keep 100% of your revenue. Set your own pricing, charge customers directly, and grow your business without revenue sharing or platform fees.
- Public marketplace listing — Once published, your integration gets featured on the Ramp Integrations page↗, giving you visibility and credibility with prospective customers.

This guide applies to all integration categories. Additional guidance for Accounting/ERP integrations is linked where relevant.

## What the Partnership Looks Like

Permanent link: What the Partnership Looks Like

Building an integration with Ramp means entering a partnership focused on delivering a high-quality experience to our shared customers. Each side plays a clear role in making that happen.

Your side:

- Pricing and monetization — You set your pricing, bill customers directly, and keep 100% of revenue. Ramp does not process payments or participate in billing.
- Building and hosting your integration — You develop and maintain your integration using Ramp's APIs.
- Customer support — You assist customers through your own support channels and provide a public support email.
- Documentation — You host setup guides, workflow instructions, and troubleshooting on your site.
- Marketing assets — You supply the logo, descriptions, screenshots, and videos for your listing.

Ramp's side:

- API troubleshooting & advisory — Our team helps you debug API issues and offers guidance on best practices and specific use cases.
- Product review and guidance — We review your integration flows and provide feedback. Approval is required before production access.
- Distribution — Your integration reaches 50,000+ businesses once published on the Ramp Integrations page.

This partnership model gives you full ownership of your product while Ramp provides oversight, guidance, and reach.

## Launch checklist

Permanent link: Launch checklist

Each integration must go through the following four stages; below is a checklist to help you work your way through each stage.

Build: Develop and test in a sandbox environment

Production Access: Apply for production access

Beta Testing: Onboard customers in a production environment

Listing: Get listed on ramp.com/integrations

### Phase 1: Build

Need a test environment for development? Request sandbox access

Use the button above to request access to the sandbox environment

Make your first API call Follow the Quickstart guide to make your first API call

Review relevant implementation guides based on your use case: ERP Integrations, Embedded Cards, Vault API, Cards

Define OAuth2 scopes and redirect URLs

Document which API scopes your integration needs and your OAuth2 redirect URLs

Implement OAuth2 Authorization Code Flow

Build the OAuth2 handoff to authenticate customers - see Authorization Code Flow guide

Test end-to-end flows in Sandbox Validate all key workflows work correctly before production

Set up integration monitoring Implement error tracking and alerting for your integration

### Phase 2: Apply for Production Access

Ready to apply for production access?

Open the technology partnerships application. Opening it does not submit your application.

Disable password login in developer console

Set up SSO↗ or other secure authentication method for your developer account

Choose integration name and description

Pick your integration name and write a clear description (you can change these later)

Record demo video with voiceover

Create a walkthrough video showing OAuth2 handoff and core user flows, clearly demonstrating where each requested API scope is used

Prepare security documentation

Gather all required security materials - see Security Requirements

Submit production access application

Open the technology partnerships application. Complete and submit the form to apply for production access.

### Phase 3: Beta Testing

Onboard 3+ beta customers

Successfully onboard at least 3 customers into production using OAuth2

Validate end-to-end data flows

Confirm all key workflows work correctly with real production data

Gather and address customer feedback

Collect beta user feedback on usability and stability, then iterate

### Phase 4: Apply for a Public Listing

Prepare logo 1024x1024px, transparent PNG or SVG format

Write description

Create a clear, compelling description that explains your integration's value to customers

Prepare marketing screenshots Capture high-quality screenshots showcasing your integration

Define pricing model (optional)

Document your pricing strategy if charging for your integration - see Pricing Guidance

Set up support email and SLAs

Create a dedicated support email alias and define response time commitments

Create internal support guidelines

Provide documentation to help Ramp's support team assist your customers

Finalize public documentation Complete customer docs - see Writing Great Documentation

Submit listing application Submit your listing application from the developer console

...

### Pricing guidance (optional)

You control your pricing. Ramp does not charge fees or take a revenue share. Many integrations are free, while others charge for their services—the choice is yours.

Best practices for pricing:

- Price relative to the value your integration delivers to customers.
- Keep pricing predictable and easy to understand.
- Factor in implementation cost, ongoing maintenance, and support burden.

Common pricing models include:

- Flat annual subscription.
- Implementation fee plus annual renewal.
- Usage-based pricing (for example, per transaction or per bill).
- Tiered feature bundles based on functionality.

gate.title: Sandbox — Ramp API docs
highlights:
Sandbox

The Ramp sandbox is a testing environment where developers and partners can safely build, test, and experiment with Ramp's API without affecting live production data.

Key features:

- Safe testing environment: Test integrations and applications before deploying to production
- API development: Access Ramp's Developer API for building custom integrations
- No real money movement: Demo accounts cannot process actual financial transactions

## How to get sandbox access

### Sandbox environments

Permanent link: Sandbox environments

| Resource | URL | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ramp frontend | https://demo.ramp.com↗ | Access the Ramp user interface for testing |
| API | https://demo-api.ramp.com↗ | Base URL for API calls in the Sandbox environment |

## Test demo actions

While building with the dev API, we support simulation actions to support testing within the Ramp sandbox environment. You can simulate user events through the demo actions panel. You can open the demo actions panel directly within the Ramp sandbox with ⌘ J.

### Mark bill as paid

Permanent link: Mark bill as paid

To mark a bill as paid, navigate to Bill Pay via the UX, then open the bill you want to mark as paid. Press ⌘ J to open the demo actions panel and select 'pay current bill'.

Note: This demo action depends on your Bill Pay payment release setting. When enabled, it only works for bills that are approved and scheduled. When disabled, it works for all bills.

For more information, see Bill Pay payment release documentation.

### Mark reimbursement as paid

Permanent link: Mark reimbursement as paid

...

### Create transaction

Permanent link: Create transaction

To create a transaction, you can do this from any page within the sandbox environment. Press ⌘ J to open the demo actions panel and click on "add transactions".

### Required permissions

Permanent link: Required permissions

Each demo action requires specific permissions to work properly:

| Action | Required Permissions |
| --- | --- |
| Mark bill as paid | Admin or Business Owner role, or the AP Clerk permission |
| Mark reimbursement as paid | A role with permission to manage reimbursement payments for the employee, such as an Admin, Bookkeeper, or an eligible manager |
| Create transaction | Employee role or higher (Manager, Admin, or Bookkeeper). The Employee role allows users to request spend, receive cards, make purchases, and submit reimbursements. View-only Admins and Guests cannot create transactions. |

gate.title: Introducing Ramp’s Technology Partner Program
highlights:
Published: July 28, 2026

# Introducing Ramp’s Technology Partner Program

David Lowes

Head of Technology Partnerships and Strategic Initiatives, Ramp

...

That’s why today we’re relaunching the Ramp Technology Partner Program: a clearer way to build with Ramp, refer customers to Ramp, and grow alongside Ramp. Th

...

## Three ways to partner with Ramp

Not every partner needs an integration. Not every partner needs the same business model. The program is designed around three ways to work with Ramp.

### Referral: Make the introduction. Earn when customers choose Ramp.

Your customers already ask you for recommendations on the tools that run their business. If Ramp is the right answer for their spend management, cards, payments, or financial operations, you can make that introduction without building anything including through a cloud marketplace co-sell motion, where eligible.

Referral partners earn on qualified customer conversions, with referral bonuses available for eligible partners and their referred customers. It is the simplest path into the program: no technical lift, a clear value-add for your customers, and real participation in the growth you create.

### Integration: Build an integration. Get discovered.

If your product becomes more useful when it connects to Ramp, build the integration and make it available to the businesses already looking for it.

Whether you're building an MCP connector, hooking into our procurement workflow, or working with spend controls and provisioning — integration partners can be listed in Ramp’s integration directory, helping their product reach more than 70,000 businesses that use Ramp to simplify their finances. You bring the workflow your customers depend on. Ramp brings the financial data and actions that make that workflow more complete.

### Embedded: Bring Ramp’s financial automation into your product.

For partners building deeper financial experiences, Ramp’s APIs make it possible to bring financial automation directly into your product.

This is the path for teams that want to build closer to the moment a customer needs to issue a card, enforce a policy, access financial data, or move money. We will share more as this program evolves.

## A partner program built to grow with you

# Connecting

There are three ways to connect your agents to Ramp:

MCP, CLI, and API connection options

| Criterion | CLI | MCP Connectors | API |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Set up | CLI Instant | MCP Connectors Instant to 15 minutes | API Hours to days |
| How it runs | CLI In a terminal, local agent, script, or CI | MCP Connectors Inside a conversational assistant | API In deterministic code |
| Permission and Attribution | CLI Actions are attributed to the acting user or agent. The agent acts as the Ramp user who authenticated the connection. Permissions do not exceed the user or agent's role. | MCP Connectors Actions are attributed to the acting user or agent. The agent acts as the Ramp user who authenticated the connection. Permissions do not exceed the user or agent's role. | API Access is limited to the scopes granted to your app. |
| Strengths | CLI Structured output, broad workflows, and easy local automation | MCP Connectors Easy setup, already available in some cases, and instant with Claude chat or an out-of-the-box connector | API Maximum control over interfaces, workflows, and backend logic |
| Weaknesses | CLI Requires installation and access to a coding agent or terminal | MCP Connectors Slower performance | API Requires the most engineering, security, and lifecycle ownership |

Use the Ramp app when a person needs to review context, handle an exception, or complete work directly. The Agent Tools reference lists every tool available in the CLI and MCP.

...

## Connect via MCP

Choose the client you already use. Each link opens the fastest available way to add Ramp.

Claude Connect Ramp in Claude and authorize the Ramp account you want the assistant to use.→ ChatGPT Add the Ramp app in ChatGPT and complete browser authorization.→ Cursor Install Ramp MCP in Cursor with one click, then authorize your Ramp account.→ Other MCP clients Connect another client or gateway using Ramp's hosted server URL.→

### Coding agents

```
# Claude Code
claude mcp add --transport http ramp https://mcp.ramp.com/mcp
 
# Codex
codex mcp add ramp --url https://mcp.ramp.com/mcp
```

Coding agents can also use the CLI.

## What the connection can do

The connection acts as the Ramp user who authorized it and never exceeds that user's permissions. On the consent screen, the user chooses Full access or Read-only. Connections expire after 30 days; reconnect to renew. Admins control who can connect with the Manage connections to Ramp via MCP, CLI and other AI connectors role permission and can revoke connections; revoking one cuts off every AI tool that shares it. See Manage connected AI tools.

## Developer API

Use the API when your product owns the interface and backend workflow. Your team is responsible for OAuth, scopes, webhooks, retries, and the customer experience.

View API reference

## Custom MCP clients

Point the client at `https://mcp.ramp.com/mcp`. For the Ramp sandbox (demo.ramp.com, the same environment as the CLI's `--env sandbox`), use `https://demo-mcp.ramp.com/mcp`. Clients that read MCP JSON usually expect:

```
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "ramp": {
      "url": "https://mcp.ramp.com/mcp"
    }
  }
}
```

Custom clients and gateways need their exact redirect URI allowlisted before authorization can complete:

- Use `https://`, or `http://` only with `localhost` or `127.0.0.1`. Ramp also accepts the `claude://`, `cursor://`, `grokbot://`, and `perplexity-app://` schemes; other custom schemes are not supported.
- Submit the exact host. Wildcard subdomains are not supported.
- Request redirect URI access for the client or gateway.

...

### A query returns too much data

Reporting queries return up to 1,000 rows per page. Narrow the date range or filters, or ask the agent to page through the results.

mcp.title: README.md
highlights:
# ramp-mcp: A Ramp MCP server

## Overview

A Model Context Protocol server for retrieving and analyzing data or running tasks for Ramp using Developer API. In order to get around token and input size limitations, this server implements a simple ETL pipeline + ephemeral sqlite database in memory for analysis by an LLM. All requests are made to demo by default, but can be changed by setting `RAMP_ENV=prd`. Large datasets may not be processable due to API and/or your MCP client limitations.

### Tools

#### Database tools

Tools that can be used to setup, process, query, and delete an ephemeral database in memory.

1. `process_data`
2. `execute_query`
3. `clear_table`

#### Fetch tools

Tools that can be used to fetch data directly

1. `get_ramp_categories`
2. `get_currencies`

#### Load tools

Loads data to server which the client can fetch. Based on the tools you wish to use, ensure to enable those scopes on your
Ramp client and include the scopes when starting the server as a CLI argument.

| Tool                      | Scope               |
| ------------------------- | ------------------- |
| load_transactions         | transactions:read   |
| load_reimbursements       | reimbursements:read |
| load_bills                | bills:read          |
| load_locations            | locations:read      |
| load_departments          | departments:read    |
| load_bank_accounts        | bank_accounts:read  |
| load_vendors              | vendors:read        |
| load_vendor_bank_accounts | vendors:read        |
| load_entities             | entities:read       |
| load_spend_limits         | limits:read         |
| load_spend_programs       | spend_programs:read |
| load_users                | users:read          |

For large datasets, it is recommended to explicitly prompt Claude not to use REPL and to keep responses concise to avoid timeout or excessive token usage.

## Setup

### Ramp Setup

1. Create a new client from the Ramp developer page (Profile on top right > Developer > Create app)
2. Grant the scopes you wish (based on tools) to the client and enable client credentials (Click on App > Grant Types / Scopes)
3. Include the client ID and secret in the config file as well as the scopes you wish to use

### Local Setup

1. Clone this Github repo via `git clone git@github.com:ramp/ramp-mcp.git` or equivalent
2. Install `uv`

## Usage

Run the MCP server from your CLI with:

```bash
RAMP_CLIENT_ID=... RAMP_CLIENT_SECRET=... RAMP_ENV=<demo|prd> uv run ramp-mcp -s <COMMA-SEPARATED-SCOPES>
```

We built a `Ramp MCP` server that lets you interact with your business data using natural language—by turning our developer API into a SQL interface that an LLM can query.

...

## What MCP is and how we used it

Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open-source standard developed by Anthropic that enables applications to expose data and functionality to LLMs. MCP provides an LLM with access to pretty much anything you want: databases, your computer’s filesystem, Figma, GitHub, etc. Given that Ramp’s developer API is the primary way to access Ramp’s resources externally, we wanted to see what would happen if we put the two together.

An MCP server in Python can be built using `FastMCP`. MCP "tools" are akin to HTTP endpoints the LLM can access through an MCP client.

...

Using `FastMCP` and a lightweight Ramp developer API client, we were able to build a working early prototype of the Ramp MCP server. With Claude Desktop as our MCP client, Claude was able to both generate visualizations and run simple analyses on spend data pulled from Ramp’s APIs using natural language. Adding a new source of data — like a different API endpoint — was as simple as defining a new tool. As a proof of concept, we had it issue cards on demand for a company offsite.

## LLMs are surprisingly good at SQL

Our initial setup worked fine on a small demo business, but we quickly ran into a few scaling issues: miscalculations, limited context windows, input size limits, and high input token usage. At first we hacked together a simple pagination tool to chunk responses into smaller, digestible parts, but we struggled to scale meaningfully beyond a few hundred transactions. Then we asked Claude what it would prefer the data to look like, and it said it preferred predictable data formats that enabled server-side functions. That sounded like SQL: structured, predictable, and built for querying. Most importantly, Claude could now load as little raw data into its context window as possible, making the server do most of the heavy computational lifting. Thanks to the reduced token usage in this approach, Ramp MCP now even worked with the free version of Claude.

Everything aside from Developer API is running locally

In order to implement a SQL interface to analyze our API data, we built a lightweight in-memory ETL that pulls data from our APIs, transforms it, and loads it into an in-memory SQLite database.

To transform our RESTful API’s JSON responses into SQL rows, we flattened the JSON and inferred the appropriate SQL column type based on the value types. To keep things simple, we set missing keys as `NULL` and cast lists to text.

```bash
{"id": 10, "amount": 123, "user": {"id": 1, "cardholder_first_name": "Eric"}}

```

becomes

```bash
id      | user_cardholder_first_name | user_id | amount
10      | "Eric"                     | 1       | 123

```

Reporting use cases involve a ton of data and complex queries, often leading to timeouts. As a solve, we added an interface to an OLAP-powered API built by our data platform team. This allowed us to extract spend data which was specifically optimized for reporting use cases, solving the timeouts.

To expose all of this functionality to the LLM, we defined a few different tools:

1. Several “load” tools (e.g. `load_transactions`) to pull data from the Ramp API
2. A `process_data` tool to transform the data from the API and load into the SQLite table (we could've skipped this step to reduce roundtrips)
3. An `execute_query` to run queries on the in-memory database directly

After this move to a SQL-based paradigm, Claude went from struggling with a few hundred data points to accurately analyzing tens of thousands of spend events. It can now load as little or as much data as it needs while running aggregate or window functions to gain a better understanding of the data. With these changes, the latency for extracting data from the API became the largest bottleneck as tool calls started timing out.

Claude querying Ramp spend data from an in-memory SQLite database

LLMs are significantly better at SQL than at math, which is why this set of tools made sense for our RESTful API to expose relational spend data effectively. MCP allows you to create whatever interface works best for the type of data you want to connect to it, and it's on you to tinker a bit to figure out what the best data access strategy is.

## Where Ramp MCP shines (and where it breaks down)

Our open-source `ramp-mcp` server can access a business context using a variety of tools, and enable natural language access to your Ramp data. It can create curated views of your spend, identify potential cost savings, and help you navigate your business hierarchy — all while surfacing insights we hadn’t even considered.

There are still limitations. There's the occasional reliability issue, and API latency can be high for very large businesses with a lot of data. There are plenty of optimizations we could implement (concurrent requests, pulling data from the APIs asynchronously, smart caching, using DuckDB, etc.), but building a scalable, and truly reliable agentic AI requires a great deal of complex technical work beyond what MCP currently offers. Write tools can be particularly unreliable, so we'll work on a safety framework before releasing tools that can perform actions in your business on your behalf as an agentic LLM.

## Ramp MCP and Audit Logs

MCP and similar technologies can introduce information security risk if left unchecked. LLMs can pull and understand large amounts of data from any source at their disposal. This means authentication credentials like API keys need to be secured, and following the principle of least privilege is as crucial as ever. As a mitigant, we implemented audit logging and you can pick a constrained set of OAuth scopes and tools to make available to the MCP client.

Audit logs for the Ramp developer API

Keep in mind that LLMs themselves may not always pick the correct tools, or they may use them incorrectly. Prompt engineering may alleviate some of this issue, but in our testing Claude occasionally made mistakes even when given the same prompt twice across separate conversations.
